name: Rhinoplasty

lead: Rhinoplasty is plastic surgery that changes the shape, size or proportions of the nose, or improves breathing. People seek it to reduce a dorsal hump, narrow the nostrils or tip, or change the nasolabial angle, and in looksmaxxing communities the nose is treated as a central feature of facial harmony. It is also done for functional reasons and for reconstruction after injury, birth defects or cancer.

Surgeons reshape the nasal bones and cartilages, adding, removing or repositioning tissue, sometimes with cartilage grafted from the septum, ear or rib. Published sources describe a long-established operation with high reported satisfaction in several studies.

paras: Surgery is done by a plastic or facial plastic surgeon, through incisions inside the nose (closed) or with an added incision across the columella (open). Preservation techniques try to keep the existing dorsum rather than cutting it down. Swelling settles gradually, and the final shape is judged after up to a year.

Reported complications include breathing impairment, asymmetry, collapse of tip support and prolonged swelling that can take up to a year to resolve; smoking impairs healing. Revision surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of operations and is technically harder. Body dysmorphic disorder is more common among cosmetic surgery patients and is associated with dissatisfaction, which is why screening is recommended.

angle.text: Rhinoplasty reshapes the nose, and the change in size and proportions is visible and measurable after healing. It is discussed as the main facial-harmony operation; the idea that nose changes shift the look of the whole face is forum opinion.

lead: Rhinoplasty, informally a 'nose job', is plastic surgery that changes the shape, size or proportions of the nose or improves its function. It takes two broad forms: reconstructive surgery, which restores form and function after injury, birth defects or failed earlier surgery, and cosmetic surgery, which changes appearance [1]. Surgery limited to the septum is called septoplasty [1][2]. People use cosmetic rhinoplasty to change how the nose sits in the face: reducing a dorsal hump, refining or rotating the tip, narrowing the nostrils or bridge, or altering the nasolabial angle, so that the nose looks more in proportion with the eyes, lips and chin [1].

The operation has an unusually long history. Nasal repair is described in the Edwin Smith Papyrus and the Sushruta Samhita of ancient India, Gasparo Tagliacozzi published a manual of nose reconstruction in 1597, John Orlando Roe reported a modern endonasal operation in 1887, and Jacques Joseph reported correcting a hump nose through internal incisions in 1904 [1][3][4]. Techniques now include open and closed approaches, cartilage grafting, ultrasonic (piezoelectric) bone cutting, dorsal preservation and filler-based nonsurgical rhinoplasty [1][5][6][7].

Within looksmaxxing forums, rhinoplasty is among the most discussed surgeries, often described as a change in 'facial harmony' and compared against jaw surgery and fillers [8][9]. Published sources report that revision surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of cases and that swelling can last up to a year [1]. A 2016 systematic review put the weighted prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder in general cosmetic surgery settings at 13.2%, and researchers recommend screening candidates [10]. Rhinoplasty has also been a visible topic on social media, including the 2021 #NoseJobCheck trend on TikTok [1].
infobox: Nose job; septorhinoplasty when combined with septal surgery [1][2]
Septal, ear or rib cartilage; diced cartilage [1][15][16]
Can persist at least a year [1]
Psychological assessment of motivation advised; BDD screening recommended [1][10]

paras: Rhinoplasty can address function, appearance or both. Functional goals include relieving obstruction through septoplasty, turbinate reduction or spreader grafts; cosmetic goals include reducing a hump, refining the tip and changing nasal angles; reconstructive uses include repair after trauma, birth defects, cancer, autoimmune damage, intranasal drug damage and failed primary surgery [1]. Specialised reviews cover non-Caucasian rhinoplasty, feminisation rhinoplasty, dorsal preservation, cleft rhinoplasty, functional rhinoplasty and nonsurgical (filler-based) rhinoplasty [5][6][11][7][12][13].

Septoplasty, the straightening of a deviated septum, is a related but separate operation. Wikipedia describes it as performed through the nostrils to relieve airway obstruction, recurrent sinusitis or septal-spur nosebleeds, and says it does not by itself change the outer shape of the nose [2]. A septorhinoplasty combines septal work with reshaping of the external nose [1].

Wikipedia traces nasal repair to the Edwin Smith Papyrus, dated to the Old Kingdom (about 3000-2500 BCE), and describes the Ebers Papyrus (about 1550 BCE) as covering reconstruction of a nose lost to rhinectomy, a punishment of the period. The Indian text attributed to Sushruta describes rebuilding a nose with a flap of cheek skin, and the Roman author Celsus covered nasal correction in De Medicina around 14 CE [1].

Gasparo Tagliacozzi (1545-1599) of Bologna refined the so-called Italian method of nasal reconstruction, using skin from the upper arm, and set it out in his 1597 book on the surgery of mutilation by grafting; Wikipedia notes that critics objected to months of arm immobilisation and that the method fell out of use in the 1600s before Karl Ferdinand von Graefe revived it around 1800 [4]. Von Graefe's 1818 Rhinoplastik reviewed historical procedures and described a free-graft technique, and Johann Friedrich Dieffenbach, an early user of anaesthesia in nose surgery, published his operative surgery text in 1845 [1].

Modern aesthetic rhinoplasty is usually dated to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. John Orlando Roe performed an endonasal operation for saddle nose deformity in 1887, and an 1894 report described surgery that would gratify the vanity of a patient with a large nose, evidence that cosmetic motives were already present [1]. Jacques Joseph, born in Konigsberg in 1865 and later head of a facial plastic surgery department at the Charite in Berlin from 1916, reported correcting a hump nose and the front of the septum through internal incisions in 1904, argued that cosmetic surgery was justified by its effect on a person's spirit and personality, and completed a two-volume book on nasal surgery in 1931 [3].

Submucous resection of the septum was pioneered by Freer and Killian in 1902-1904, Aurel Rethi introduced the open approach in 1934, and Maurice Cottle's 1947 hemitransfixion incision supported closed, septum-preserving work [1]. Open rhinoplasty was popularised in the 1970s-1990s by Padovan, Wilfred Goodman and Jack Gunter, with Gunter reporting on secondary rhinoplasty in 1987, and Massimo Robiony introduced ultrasonic rhinoplasty in 2004 [1].

Surgeons divide the nose into nine aesthetic subunits and six segments to map a defect or deformity, and Wikipedia says that when more than half of a subunit is lost the whole segment is usually replaced [1]. Ideal proportions cited in the article include a nose occupying about one third of facial height and one fifth of facial width, a nasofrontal angle of about 115-130 degrees (more acute in men), a nasolabial angle of 90-95 degrees in men and 100-105 degrees in women, and about 2 mm of columellar show [1]. Tip projection is assessed with ratios such as the Goode method (0.55:1 to 0.60:1), and the 10-7-5 method lists the frontal, lateral and basal features to review; three-dimensional imaging is also used in planning [1].

These are the same angles looksmaxxing posters discuss when they describe 'nasofrontal', 'nasolabial' and tip rotation [8]. Wikipedia also says patient evaluation includes a medical history, a physical exam that includes the Cottle manoeuvre for internal valve collapse, and an assessment of the patient's psychological motivation [1].

Surgery is performed under sedation, general or local anaesthesia [1]. In open rhinoplasty a columellar incision is added to the usual internal incisions, giving better visibility and tip control and generally being preferred for revision surgery. Closed rhinoplasty keeps all incisions inside the nose and involves less dissection, less swelling and scarring, a shorter operation and faster recovery. Wikipedia reports that systematic reviews found no significant long-term difference in functional or aesthetic outcome scores between the two, and that surgeon expertise and anatomy drive the choice [1].

Grafts of cartilage from the septum, ear or rib, or of bone, support the nose; septal cartilage is preferred, and synthetic implants are used when autologous tissue is unavailable [1]. Septal extension grafts, described in a 1997 paper, offer more control of tip projection than columellar struts [1][14]. Diced cartilage wrapped in Surgicel, the 'Turkish delight' graft, was reported in 2000 by Erol, who described using it in 2,365 patients over ten years to avoid the visible edges of carved cartilage [15]; a 2004 prospective study by Daniel examined 50 consecutive diced cartilage grafts in primary and secondary rhinoplasty [16]. A 2006 paper reviewed concepts in tip contouring [17].

Ultrasonic (piezoelectric) instruments cut bone while sparing soft tissue, a technique introduced by Massimo Robiony in 2004 [1]. Dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, which keeps the existing nasal dorsum instead of removing a hump and rebuilding it, has been the subject of a 2024 surgical review in which several named surgeons debate indications and challenges [6]. After surgery, noses are taped and splinted, with dressings typically removed at about a week [1].

Wikipedia groups nasal anatomy into African (platyrrhine), Asiatic (subplatyrrhine), Caucasian (leptorrhine) and Hispanic (paraleptorrhine) types and notes that thick skin in some noses makes open surgery more useful for securing cartilage; a 2009 study proposed classifying tips by skin thickness [1]. A 2022 review treats non-Caucasian rhinoplasty as an important patient group [5]. Reviews also address feminisation rhinoplasty within gender-affirming care [11], cleft rhinoplasty [18] and functional rhinoplasty [13].

Nonsurgical rhinoplasty uses injectable fillers to alter the profile, and reviews describe rising demand for less invasive options as filler technology and injection technique have improved [7][12]. Forum members frequently contrast these temporary changes with surgical reshaping [8].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, reports satisfaction of roughly 89-93% in several studies of rib-cartilage and hybrid techniques, about 75-85% satisfaction after revision surgery, and a 2018 blinded observer study of 473 raters in which rhinoplasty improved perceived attractiveness, success and health; these figures are unsourced in the entry and are best read against primary papers [19]. The same entry gives the nasofrontal angle at about 115-130 degrees and describes tip projection ratios [19].

Outcome measurement is a research field in its own right. The Glasgow Benefit Inventory, an 18-item questionnaire developed in 1996, measures patient benefit after ear, nose and throat interventions [20], and reviews of outcomes research in facial plastic and aesthetic surgery appeared in 2000 and 2003, with a 2001 pilot study of cosmetic facial plastic surgery outcomes [21][22][23].

Wikipedia notes that over-aggressive surgery can impair breathing and cause asymmetry, collapse, a pinched tip or a scooped profile, that swelling can take at least a year to resolve, and that smoking impairs healing [1]. A single dose of corticosteroid has limited evidence of reducing swelling and bleeding for the first two days [1]. Secondary rhinoplasty is needed in about 5-20% of operations and is harder because support structures are often damaged in the first operation [1]. Named deformities in the literature include pollybeak, saddle nose, inverted-V and open roof deformity [1].

Grokipedia reports overall complication rates of about 4-18.8%, mostly minor, with infection around 1-2%, septal perforation about 2% and mortality under 0.01%, and says a 2025 meta-analysis of ethnicity-tailored approaches found fewer complications and revisions than conventional methods; these figures should be verified against primary sources [19]. For septal surgery, Wikipedia lists excessive bleeding in about 1% of patients, septal haematoma or perforation, temporary numbness of the upper front teeth and, after over-resection, saddle nose [2].

A 2016 systematic review in Body Image estimated the weighted prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder at 1.9% in community adults, 2.2% in adolescents, 3.3% in students and 13.2% in general cosmetic surgery settings [10]. Wikipedia's article on the disorder reports that people with it often seek cosmetic or dermatological treatment, that surgery often does not relieve their distress, that cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRIs are considered effective treatments, and that surgeons and psychiatrists are encouraged to screen patients together [24]. It also links 'Snapchat dysmorphia', patients seeking surgery to resemble filtered photos, with rising interest [24].

Grokipedia reports that BDD affects up to about 15% of cosmetic surgery patients and that untreated BDD is associated with dissatisfaction and multiple revisions [19]. Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article says surgeons assess a patient's psychological motivation before operating [1].

Wikipedia reports that between October 2020 and January 2021 the #NoseJobCheck audio was used in more than 120,000 TikTok videos and the hashtag collected over a billion views, with creators posting before-and-after reveals of rhinoplasty results [1]. In looksmaxxing forums, posters name celebrities they say were improved by nose refinement and trade 'morph' images that edit a photo to preview a new nose [8][25].

Forum posters also discuss practical questions: whether European surgeons or surgeons in Korea and Japan suit a given nose, with one reply saying Korean and Japanese surgeons are better known for Asian rhinoplasty and that grafted projection work suits European centres [26]. On T Nation, a poster in 2009 said insurance covered septum repair but not cosmetic rhinoplasty after a broken nose, and a 2007 thread described a reported trend of men seeking noses that looked more masculine [27][28].

Forum members present the nose as central to midface harmony. One long looksmax.org thread argues that wide alar bases, weak projection or ski-slope bridges limit a face, that fillers only camouflage while rhinoplasty permanently reshapes bone and cartilage, and names celebrities it says benefited, and another user pointed out that the examples were all women [8]. Other threads debate rhinoplasty against jaw surgery for a 'pretty boy' look [9], argue that rhinoplasty is 'cope' for men [29], collect rhinoplasty 'morphs' [25], collect nose ideas [30], say rhinoplasty can be the best harmony surgery when done well [31], report disappointing results [32] or question why many Asian rhinoplasty results look unnatural [33]. In one thread an 18-year-old describes being offered a free rhinoplasty when only a septoplasty was medically needed and asks whether to take it, with a reply saying a free operation is still free [34].

Randomised and controlled trials in rhinoplasty have mostly studied perioperative issues rather than aesthetic outcomes. Examples in the published record include a 1994 trial on the nasal hinge [35], a 1989 double-blind pilot of steroids versus placebo for swelling and bruising [36], a 1997 trial of clonidine as premedication [37], a 2023 trial on the effects of burr-assisted rhinoplasty on hearing [38], a 2024 trial of peroperative cooling [39] and a 2026 double-blind trial on postoperative pain management [40]. Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include a completed 2024 trial of step count and edema after rhinoplasty with 124 participants [41], a completed 92-participant trial of a columella strut's effect on tip rotation [42] and a completed 100-participant trial examining preservation rhinoplasty and nasal valve angle and area [43].

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums rhinoplasty is regarded as a high-impact facial surgery, with long threads on technique, morphs, surgeon choice and results [8][9][32].

claims.claim: The nose drives midface harmony, so reshaping it changes the whole face.
Fillers only camouflage, while surgery permanently reshapes bone and cartilage.
Rhinoplasty can go wrong and make a face look worse or 'fake'.
European surgeons are better for grafted projection work, while Korea and Japan suit Asian noses.
A free rhinoplasty is worth taking even if only a septoplasty is needed.
Surgery fixes the underlying dissatisfaction with one's looks.
